background.definition: The porphyrias are a collection of diseases caused by abnormalities in heme biosynthesis. Mutations at each step of the heme biosynthesis pathway are associated with a specific type of porphyria. The porphyrias can be broadly broken into two categories, the hepatic porphyrias and the erythropoietic porphyrias. This topic focuses on the hepatic porphyrias.

list.listitem: The incidence of the porphyrias varies widely throughout the world. They are more common in Northern European populations. A 3-year prospective study found an annual incidence rate of 1.3 cases/100,000 per year in most European countries for symptomatic acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), but a higher rate in Sweden (5.1 cases/100,000 per year).
Variegate porphyria (VP) is common among the Afrikaner population in South Africa, with some estimations of incidence of 1/500.

The hepatic porphyrias are genetically determined, but with variable penetrance. Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), hereditary coporphyria (HCP), and variegate porphyria (VP) are autosomal dominant with variable penetrance. ALA dehydrogenase porphyria (ALADP) is autosomal recessive.
It is most common among women age 15 to 50 years.
Steroid hormones, especially estrogens, can trigger acute attacks of the hepatic porphyrias.
Medications including barbiturates, hormone therapy (including oral contraceptives), sulfonamides, atazanavir/ritonavir, as well as alcohol ingestion, can trigger acute porphyria attacks.
Metabolites of nicotine can trigger attacks of AIP.
Each of the intermediate metabolites involved in heme biosynthesis is toxic in excess.
The porphyrins that cause the hepatic porphyrias are neuro-visceral toxins that cause abdominal pain and neuro-psychiatric symptoms, including headaches, seizures, weakness, and sensory disturbances.
Patients with the porphyrias are asymptomatic until exposed to a trigger for their specific disease.
Care in selecting medications is a key to preventing attacks in acute porphyria. C
Screening family members of case patients for the porphyrias has been suggested, but there is no evidence that it decreases morbidity. The USPSTF does not address the question. C
Consider porphyrias when evaluating patients with recurrent abdominal pain or neuro-psychaitric abnormalities, including seizures, peripheral neuropathies, and paralysis. C
The initial test of choice is random urine porphobilinogen and omega-aminolevulinic acid corrected to creatinine.C

list.listitem: Presenting symptoms depend on the specific type of porphyria. In a case series of 36 Chinese patients with acute porphyria, adominal pain (32 of 36) was the most common presenting symptom and hyponatremia (29 of 36) as the most common lab abnormality.

The acute hepatic porphyrias, including [ALA dehydrogenase porphyria (ALADP), acute intermittent porphyria (AIP), hereditary coporphyria (HCP), and variegate porphyria (VP) present with episodic abdominal pain (85% of cases)] and neuro-psychiatric symptoms. Urine darkens in color to orange or red on exposure to light, and patients may have nausea, vomiting, and constipation (British Guidelines).

The neuro-psychiatric symptoms can include headaches, limb pain, proximal muscle weakness, seizures, sensory disturbances, including peripheral neuropathy and weakness that can mimic Guillain-Barre syndrome.

The acute hepatic porphyrias are generally asymptomatic until after puberty. The sex steroids, especially estrogens, are implicated in triggering attacks. These porphyrias frequently exacerbate with the menstrual cycle.
Symptomatic hepatic porphyrias are more common in women due to the inciting nature of estrogens.

The acute hepatic porphyrias are often triggered by starvation or calorie deprivation. Dieting for weight loss or being made NPO following surgery are common triggers for acute attacks. Stress or alcohol use have also been implicated as triggers, as has sun exposure.
Medications or drugs, including alcohol, sulfonamides, barbiturates, and oral contraceptives are common triggers for acute attacks.

The metabolic products responsible for symptoms in the hepatic porphyrias are water soluble, are excreted through the urine and should be tested for in the urine. This testing should include 24 hour urine testing for delta-aminolevulinic acids (ALA), porphobilinogen (PBG), and fecal coporphyrin. Urine samples should be protected from light.

Spot levels of urine porphobilinogen (PBG) and total porphyrin may be elevated during an acute attack. Assess urine concentration by measuring urine creatinine, and obtain another specimen if urine creatinine is less than 2 mmol/L. See and for interpretation of these results.
To diagnose cutaneous porphyria, obtain an EDTA blood sample and order plasma porphyrin fluorescence emission spectroscopy. A random sample for urine porphyrin excretion is also recommended.

More than 200 separate genetic mutations have been described that can cause acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). Genetic screening is not appropriate for initial screening, as there are many genetic mutations that can cause each specific porphyria.
Once a diagnosis of a porphyria is established, genetic testing for the specific gene mutation may help simplify case identification in asymptomatic family members.

Recommended tests for acute hepatic porphyria are random urine porphobilinogen and δ-aminolevulinic acid corrected to creatinine. If elevated, patients should be assumed to have acute hepatic porphyria.
Suspect hepatic porphyrias in patients with intermittent abdominal symptoms and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
The porphyrins responsible for the hepatic porphyrias are water soluble, and are excreted in the urine. A 24 hour urine assays for porphyrins is necessary for the diagnosis of the hepatic porphyrias
See for guidance regarding interpretation of tests in different types of hepatic prophyrias.
Calorie replacement with intravenous infusion of glucose, effective analgesia, and attention to fluid balance are the cornerstone of treatment for the acute hepatic porphyrias.C
Givosiran reduces the frequency of attacks significantly. B
Refractory cases may require infusions of hematin or haem arginate to break the acute attack. B
Prevention is an important part of the care of patients with porphyria, and care in selecting medications and avoiding other triggers is important. C

Treatment for the acute hepatic porphyrias includes removal of the inciting agent, pain management, fluid management, and reversal of calorie deprivation. Glucose infusion is often sufficient to resolve symptoms.

Givosiran in a once monthly subcutaneous injection at a dose of 2.5 mg/kg was significantly more effective than placebo in reducing the number of attacks (3.2 vs 12.5 attacks per year, p < 0.001). The proportion reporting no attacks in a year was also much higher (50% vs 17%, NNT = 3). The drug does increase the likelihood of worsening chronic kidney disease and elevation of hepatic transaminases.

In patients with persistent or severe symptoms, hematin (US) or haem/heme arginate (UK and elsewhere) infusions may be helpful. However, the only randomized trial was inconclusive. If given, infuse normal saline after infusion as it can be an irritant to veins.
Provide analgesia, such as morphine, and nausea/vomiting with drugs such as prochlorperazine or ondansetron.
Treat psychotic symptoms with chlorpromazine if severe or persistent.

Erythropoietic protoporphyria: An RCT in 168 patients found that afamelanotide 16 mg implanted subcutaneously reduced the number of phototoxic episodes over a 6 month period (77 vs 146, p = 0.04) and increased pain-free intervals in a clinically important manner.
A case series of 23 patients with porphyria cutaneous tarda and hepatis C found improvement in virologic parameters with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir treatment.
Liver transplantation is curative, but should only be considered in patients with severe and frequent attacks.

Prevention is the cornerstone of treatment for all the porphyrias. Patients should be instructed to strictly avoid inciting agents, including estrogens (including oral contraceptives), alcohol, and certain drugs such as barbiturates and sulfa antibiotics.
Smoking cessation may be of benefit in acute intermittent porphyria.
During acute attacks, monitor vitals and provide adequate intravenous hydration. Monitor neurologic function.
Always consider other causes for symptoms, such as psychiatric illness, appendicitis, or gall bladder disease.
The porphyrias produce significant morbidity, but rare mortality. C
Mortality is generally secondary to neurologic complications, including seizures and paralysis. C
The porphyrias do not generally present until after puberty. C
The incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma is 0.3 cases per 100 person-years based on a systematic review of 12 observational studies with 2735 patients.
The porphyrias generally do not present until after the onset of puberty.
